byline: A Horse-Centered Standard for Centro Equino Chichihuas · Walker Rollins · October 2026
photo_caption: Mina y Vuelta · Mina and Vuelta, daughters of the free herd
blocks: What the free herd taught me
The best horse trainers I have known were not people. They were the horses of a wild herd in northern Baja, at Rancho Las Chichihuas, where I have lived among them for years.
Nobody told those horses where to walk or when to eat. Nobody asked them to trust me. When trust came, it came because I learned to sit still, to watch, and to wait until I was invited closer.

That experience changed how I see every domestic horse. I stopped asking, “How do I get this horse to do what I want?” I started asking, “What would this horse choose, if it could?” This article is my attempt to turn that question into a standard other people can use.
Why we need a written standard

Natural horsemanship, liberty work and bitless riding have no shared, written standard. What they have instead is a crowded field of trainers, each with a brand, a method and a set of rules. Some are kind. Some use “natural” language to dress up pressure, chasing and dominance.
Meanwhile, the science has moved ahead. Three frameworks already exist, but nobody has joined them into one:

The ISES Training Principles. The International Society for Equitation Science publishes ten principles meant for any horse, in any discipline. They ask trainers to avoid pain and fear, keep sessions short, break learning into small steps, and encourage positive emotional states. ISES has also published a position statement questioning the use of leadership and dominance ideas in training.

The Five Domains Model. This is now the main tool for judging a horse’s welfare. It looks at nutrition, environment, health and behaviour, then asks what the horse is actually feeling: the fifth, mental domain.

The World Bitless Association. The WBA promotes training based on science and compassion, follows the LIMA principle (Least Intrusive, Minimally Aversive), and campaigns for riders to be free to choose bitless bridles.

Each covers part of the picture: how we train, how horses live, and what we put on their heads. This article proposes one standard that holds all three together, and measures everything against the life of a free herd.
The wild herd as the measuring stick
Every standard needs a baseline. Mine is the free herd: the clearest picture we have of what a horse is built for. Watching free horses, a few things stand out:
They move all day. Slowly, mostly walking, covering ground while they graze.
They eat little and often. Grazing and browsing take up most of their waking hours.
They live in families. Bonds are long-lasting, and a horse is almost never alone.
They choose. Where to stand, who to stand next to, when to leave. Conflict is usually solved with a look or a step, not a fight.
They rest in safety. One horse dozes while another keeps watch.

This does not mean wild life is easy. Free horses face drought, injury, hunger and loss. The goal is not to copy the wild. The goal is to meet the same needs the wild reveals: movement, forage, company and choice, without the hardship.
So the test for any barn, any training session and any piece of tack is simple: how close does it come to what the herd already knows a horse needs?
The standard rests on five pillars. Each one can be checked, and each one comes back to the herd.
How a horse lives matters more than any hour of training. Using the Five Domains as a guide, a horse-centered home provides:
Forage available most of the day, and clean water always
Room to move, ideally with turnout every day and not just a stall
Company: horses who can see, smell and touch each other
Shelter from sun, wind and rain, with a choice to use it
Regular care for hooves, teeth and body condition
When these needs are met, the fifth domain, the horse’s own feeling, usually follows: calm, curious, willing.
Connection comes before any task. It means presence before technique: arriving quietly, breathing slowly, letting the horse notice you first.
It also means consent. A horse should be able to say yes, and to say no. Turning away, moving off, stiffening or freezing are answers, not disobedience. A good trainer listens to them and adjusts.
Small steps, each one made easy and clear
No pain, no fear, no fighting
Low arousal: a calm horse learns, a frightened one only survives
No “dominance” or “alpha” thinking. Horses do not need us to be their boss. They need us to be clear, consistent and safe.
A note on the round pen. Under this standard, the round pen is a place to talk, not to drive. If a horse is running from you, the lesson has already gone wrong.
Liberty work, with no rope, halter or bridle, is the truest test of a relationship. A horse at liberty can always leave. If it stays, follows and works with you, that choice means something.
Liberty is not a trick or a show. It is where the relationship is built, and it should come before riding, not after.
When we ride, we use the least invasive equipment that keeps horse and rider safe. That usually means a well-fitted bitless bridle and a saddle that fits the horse’s back today, not last year.
The horse is the judge of the tack. Open mouths, tossed heads, pinned ears and a clamped tail all tell us something is wrong. We listen to that before we listen to tradition or competition rules.
A horse-centered standard is also a land standard. Horses shape the ground they live on, and the ground shapes their health. From regenerative land practice, a few principles carry over directly:
Graze in rotation. Move horses between areas so plants can recover and roots stay deep.
Protect the soil. Bare, compacted ground means dust, mud and runoff. Living ground holds water and feeds the herd.
Work with what grows. Native and established plants give shade, shelter and browse, and they cost nothing to keep.
Design for movement. Paths, water and feed placed apart encourage horses to walk, the way a herd does.

I am applying these ideas now in the design of a new equine center near Ensenada. Rather than clearing the site, the plan works around the mature plantings already there. Every stall opens onto its own run, so no horse is shut in a box, and every horse can see its neighbours. The barn is built of local stone outside and timber inside, with the aisle opening toward the hills. The arena and round pen sit within that same landscape.
For 15 years I taught regenerative land practices to children aged 6 to 16, in Los Angeles schools and on farm schools. Some of the deepest lessons came when horses were part of the day.

Children learn fast from a horse that is allowed to choose. A horse that walks away teaches patience better than any lecture. A horse that comes closer teaches them that calm, honest attention is rewarded. They learn to read body language, to slow their breathing, and to ask instead of demand.

The same spirit runs through Estrechando el Lazo, a program at Rancho Las Chichihuas that reconnects people with nature. It also offers the wild-horse visits I host each spring, where guests spend time near the herd on the herd’s terms. All proceeds from those visits go to the care of the horses.
If we want a kinder horse world, we have to start with the people who will be in it longest: the children.
Use these questions to rate your own barn, training or riding. Each “no” is a place to start.
Does my horse have forage available most of the day?
Does my horse get to move freely, every day?
Can my horse see, smell and touch other horses?
Can my horse choose shelter from sun, wind and rain?
Do I arrive calmly and let my horse notice me first?
Can my horse say no without being punished?
Are my sessions short, with small steps and clear rewards?
Do I train without pain, fear or chasing?
Will my horse stay with me with no rope or halter?
Am I using the least invasive tack that keeps us safe?
Does my horse look relaxed under saddle: soft mouth, quiet tail, soft eyes?
I did not earn my place near the wild horses by asking for it. I earned it by showing up, again and again, quietly, until I was no longer a threat or a stranger.

That is the heart of this standard. We do not take a place in a horse’s life. We earn it, through how we house them, how we teach them, what we put on their bodies, and how we listen when they answer.
The wild herd already wrote the standard. Our job is to read it, and to live up to it.
